title: Canada Probes Import Risks After India Raid Uncovers Fake Labels on Food Products
excerpt: The Canadian Food Inspection Agency is the first foreign regulator to respond after Indian authorities seized nearly $80,000 worth of relabelled PepsiCo, Nestle and Coca-Cola products from a Mumbai warehouse.
body:
• Canada's food safety agency is assessing whether expired Indian food products with fake nutrition labels and expiry dates were exported to the country.
  • Indian authorities raided a Mumbai warehouse last week, seizing products worth nearly $80,000 along with chemicals and printing machines used to forge labels for PepsiCo, Nestle, Coca-Cola and Unilever products.
  • A Kurkure packet found at the warehouse bore fake nutrition information in English and French — matching Canada's bilingual labelling format — raising export concerns.
  • The warehouse operators worked on behalf of 19 small exporters, though the destination countries remain unclear.

The Canadian Food Inspection Agency (CFIA) said Thursday it is monitoring a food fraud operation uncovered in India to determine whether tampered products reached Canadian consumers. The announcement makes Canada the first foreign government to formally respond to the Mumbai warehouse raid.

What the Raid Found

Indian authorities last week raided a warehouse in Mumbai's Navi Mumbai district, seizing products worth nearly $80,000 along with chemicals and printing machines. The equipment was being used to replace expired or near-expiry dates and alter nutritional information on branded food products from PepsiCo, Nestle, Coca-Cola and Unilever, according to Maharashtra's Food and Drug Administration.

https://x.com/CTVNews/status/2095459370049925260

"We have written to concerned authorities about our findings, who will investigate details of the exporters involved."

— Tukaram Mundhe, Maharashtra FDA Commissioner

The products were repackaged to appear suitable for export. Crucially, a Reuters photographer at the scene spotted a packet of PepsiCo's Indian brand Kurkure puffed chips bearing a fake label with nutrition information printed in both English and French — the exact bilingual format prescribed under Canadian food labelling laws.

Canada's Response

The CFIA said in a statement to Reuters that it "is monitoring the situation to determine whether it presents any risk to imports into Canada." The agency added that it currently has no information suggesting products from the operation entered the country.

"The Canadian Food Inspection Agency takes food fraud, including false date markings, inaccurate nutrition information, and misleading origin claims seriously," the statement said. If non-compliant foods are identified, the CFIA said it can pursue product removal, licence suspension and monetary penalties.

A Wider Crackdown in India

The Mumbai raid is part of an unprecedented food safety drive across India. Both federal and state authorities have been aggressively inspecting food production and distribution facilities, checking for hygiene breaches and food safety violations. Some operations have drawn instant suspension orders.

Indian officials said the Mumbai warehouse owners carried out relabelling activities on behalf of 19 little-known exporters. It remains unclear which countries the goods were destined for. The companies whose branding was misused — PepsiCo, Nestle, Coca-Cola and Unilever — have not been accused of wrongdoing.

PepsiCo told Reuters it has "no commercial engagement with the export companies referenced in recent media reports" and does not authorise or support any unauthorised export of its products. "Our snack food products manufactured in India are meant for sale in India, unless otherwise specifically authorised by us to be exported," the company said.

What It Means for Indian Exporters

The incident puts a spotlight on food export quality controls at a time when India is pushing to expand its processed food exports globally. For the Indian diaspora in Canada, it raises questions about the safety and authenticity of imported Indian food products available in ethnic grocery stores.

India's commerce ministry, which oversees exports, has not yet commented on the matter. Maharashtra's FDA commissioner said the agency has formally written to relevant authorities to investigate the exporters involved.

What Comes Next

The CFIA's assessment is ongoing, and no product recalls have been issued so far. The investigation on the Indian side is expected to trace the full export chain from the 19 identified exporters. If Canadian authorities determine that tampered products did cross the border, enforcement actions including product seizures and penalties against importers could follow.
